name: Live at the Chancellery
description: Recorded in May 2002 at The Chancellery in Charlottesville, Virginia during the 2001–2002 Across The World Tour and released in October 2002 following the debut of Crimson Node. Opens with 'The Stardust Engine', closes the main set with 'Electric Color', and culminates in the historic surprise encore where Ryan and Cassidy O'Connell officially introduce Crimson Node to the world with a joint performance of 'The Flight Path'.
subtitle: The 2001–2002 Across The World Tour — Charlottesville Arena Encore Introducing Crimson Node
linerNotes: Recorded during the post-commencement weekend of May 2002 inside The Chancellery—the 15,000-seat flagship indoor arena of The University of the Piedmont (UP, in-universe UVA) in Charlottesville, Virginia—Live at the Chancellery documents one of the most famous torch-passing moments in Engine Room Records history.

In 2002, long before the 2014 Norfolk (VDU) football rivalry began, CPI's eternal in-state blood feud was with Charlottesville's own UP Chancellors ('The Rahoos'). Yet because Albemarle County's Crimson Node were beloved labelmates and friends attending UP, The Stardust Engine rolled into The Chancellery as friends—stepping onto the stage wearing Navy Blue and Old Gold UP logo shirts instead of their trademark maroon CPI Alumni gear. After opening with 'The Stardust Engine' and closing their main set with their traditional closer 'Electric Color', Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler returned for a special encore that closed the entire concert: Ryan confessed that the mysterious unnamed song they had been road-testing on tour (including mid-concert in Virginia Beach) wasn't written by The Stardust Engine at all, and officially introduced Crimson Node to the world. Immediately after the show, Holly O'Connell worked with Crimson Node to get the studio cut of 'The Flight Path' onto Charlottesville FM rock radio, priming the city all summer before Crimson Node's debut album dropped on September 18, 2002 (finally giving fans the name of the song), followed by the release of Live at the Chancellery in October 2002 and Live in Virginia Beach in November 2002.

studioArchives.title: The Five-Step "Trojan Horse" Rollout & Holly's FM Radio Blitz (2002)
studioArchives.content: (1) At the Live in Virginia Beach concert earlier on the tour—after testing the mystery song for a few weeks on the road—The Stardust Engine plays 'The Flight Path' mid-concert to see if the Virginia Beach crowd knows the words (the first performance of the song captured for a future live album, with no song title given). (2) At the May 2002 Live at the Chancellery concert in Charlottesville, The Stardust Engine introduces Crimson Node as a band to close the night after 'Electric Color' (still without naming the song on stage), and Holly O'Connell works with Crimson Node to get the studio version onto local FM rock stations by legally purchasing post-concert midnight airtime blocks. (3) On September 18, 2002, Crimson Node's self-titled debut album drops, finally giving fans the name of the song. (4) In October 2002, Live at the Chancellery is released. (5) In November 2002, Live in Virginia Beach is released.

studioArchives.title: Friends Across the CPI vs. UP Rivalry
studioArchives.content: Although CPI ('The Forgers' / 'The Ironheads') and The University of the Piedmont ('The Chancellors' / 'The Rahoos', who sneeringly call CPI 'Comm Tech') are bitter collegiate rivals, neither the O'Connell/Wright family nor the Miller/Brooks family of Albemarle County cared for campus elitism. By taking the stage at The Chancellery in UP shirts and praising the arena's mathematically perfect acoustic baffling, The Stardust Engine turned rival territory into a unified celebration for their friends in Crimson Node.

studioArchives.title: Sacred Setlist Boundaries
studioArchives.content: Because the concert closes with the special joint encore introducing Crimson Node on 'The Flight Path', The Stardust Engine's usual concert closer 'Electric Color' is played right before the encore at Track 13. As on all independent-era Stardust Engine tours, 'If You Walked Away' is permanently retired to honor Cassidy's sensory and emotional boundaries.
